content.text:
The reporter is right that the app can't connect a Creator 5 Pro, but the cause is in the app's own chat setup, not in OrcaSlicer. OrcaSlicer's Flashforge code already supports this printer. The chat's connection step never gives it the two things it needs, so it falls back to an older method the printer rejects.

**What happens today**

Here is the sequence when the person asks the AI to connect their Creator 5 Pro:

1. The AI calls the app's connect tool, `printer_host_connect`. That tool takes only a connection type and an address ([ToolRegistry.cpp:1706](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/ToolRegistry.cpp:1706)).
2. The app tests the connection ([OrcaPrinterBackend.cpp:838](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/PrinterSetup/OrcaPrinterBackend.cpp:838)). It fills in the type, address and API key, and never the Flashforge serial number. `flashforge_serial_number` is also on the list of settings the AI may not write ([SettingsSupport.hpp:29](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Workspace/SettingsSupport.hpp:29)).
3. OrcaSlicer's `Flashforge::test` ([Flashforge.cpp:344](src/slic3r/Utils/Flashforge.cpp:344)) only uses the printer's HTTP interface on port 8898 when it has both a serial number and an access code. Without them it falls back to the older raw TCP connection on port 8899. The reporter's printer refused that connection.
4. The form where the person types an access code only opens when the printer answers HTTP 401 or 403. A refused connection is neither, so the person is never asked for the code.

The OctoPrint attempt on port 80 was never going to work, because this printer doesn't run OctoPrint. The AI guessed that type.

OrcaSlicer's own physical-printer dialog does handle this. It has a Discover button that finds Flashforge printers on the network and fills in their serial numbers ([PhysicalPrinterDialog.cpp:195](src/slic3r/GUI/PhysicalPrinterDialog.cpp:195)), plus a field for the access code. Upstream added this in OrcaSlicer PR 12991 and supports the Creator 5 and 5 Pro on that path (PR 17237). The JusPrin chat was built without that path.

**What's verified and what isn't**

- Verified by reading the code: without a serial number, the chat can only ever try port 8899 on a Flashforge printer.
- Taken from the issue, not tested by me: the Creator 5 Pro refuses port 8899. I have no Creator 5 Pro to reproduce it on. A web search turned up Flashforge's port layout (HTTP on 8898, raw TCP on 8899) only for the sibling Adventurer 5M models, not the Creator 5 Pro itself.
- My hypothesis: the same gap hits any Flashforge printer that only answers on its HTTP interface.

**What the fix would need (proposal, nothing agreed)**

1. When the connection type is Flashforge, the chat runs the same network search OrcaSlicer's Discover button uses (`Flashforge::discover_printers`) to get the serial number.
2. It opens the existing access-code form up front, the way the Bambu connect step does, instead of waiting for a 401 or 403.
3. It saves the serial number together with the address.

This adds a new step to the chat's printer setup, so the screens would need to be designed before any code, per the design guidelines.

**A possible workaround for the reporter (not checked in JusPrin's UI)**

In the classic view, they can open the physical-printer settings, choose Flashforge, click Discover, and type the access code from the printer's screen.

Nobody has replied on the issue yet.

Sources:
- [parallel-7 Flashforge API docs](https://awesome.ecosyste.ms/projects/github.com%2Fparallel-7%2Fflashforge-api-docs)

# Connecting a printer through a print host

The rules above still apply. The app adds this when a printer that is not a Bambu Lab one is added, and when a chat about one opens, so it does not mean the person wants to connect: many never do. Start connecting only once they say they want to. Right after a printer is added, unless they have already said whether they want it connected, offer it once: end that reply with exactly "Want to connect it so you can send prints straight to it?" and then "Choices: Connect it | Not now". When they have already asked to connect it, go straight on.

Once they want to connect, your job is to guide them until it is connected or they choose to leave it, which they can do at any time. This explains how the connection works, so you can work out what is going on, including in situations it does not mention. Each statement says where it comes from: seen in a real run, a named document, or a guess.

## Which connection type

printer_host_connect needs to know which program the app talks to, its `hostType`. printer_connection_status gives the type this printer is saved with. Until a connection is saved, that type is only the default in the printer's profile, which the person never chose: an Elegoo printer's profile names Elegoo Link, and a Prusa's names PrusaLink (from the app's printer profiles). Use it unless what the person says shows their printer runs something else.

- **A Klipper printer is reached through Moonraker** (`moonraker`), the program beside Klipper that other apps talk to over the network. People usually use it through a web page in a browser, Mainsail or Fluidd. The app talks only to Moonraker. A printer whose page is Mainsail or Fluidd runs Moonraker, whatever its profile says.
- **OctoPrint runs on a computer beside the printer and drives it** (`octoprint`). People use it through OctoPrint's own web page. The app talks only to OctoPrint, never to the printer itself.
- **Elegoo Link** (`elegoolink`): see below.
- **Every other type** printer_host_connect lists runs the app's own test for that type, the one the app's printer connection window runs, and has not been tried here against a real printer. Its failures come in that test's words, which may be in the app's language. The app sends an address and one key. From the app's code, these need more, and cannot be finished from this chat: Repetier, which also needs the printer chosen on the host; UltiMaker, which needs a user name and password; and PrusaLink set up with a user name and password instead of a key. The person can finish those in the app's own window for it: View › Switch to classic view…, then the Wi-Fi icon beside "Printer" (seen 2026-11-16).

When the person does not know whether they have Moonraker or OctoPrint, ask what the page they open to control the printer is called, or what it shows. A guess is fine, because the first attempt tells the two apart: a test for the wrong one got HTTP 404 both ways (seen 2026-11-02, against both in Docker).

## Elegoo Link

From the app's code for Elegoo Link (read 2026-11-16). It tells Elegoo printers apart by the model the person picked in the app, not by asking the printer:

- **Centauri Carbon.** The test asks for the printer's own web page at the address, and passes when that page contains "ELEGOO". It uses no key. "ElegooLink not detected" means something answered there, but not with that page. The address is the printer's IP address, with no port. OctoEverywhere's help pages for the Centauri printers say the printer's touchscreen shows it, in its settings on the Network tab, under the network it is connected to, and that a Centauri Carbon 2 also shows it at the lower left of its home screen, after "IP:" (read 2026-11-16).
- **Centauri Carbon 2.** The test asks the printer for its information with an access code, and with none it sends 123456. A refused code got HTTP 401 or 403, and then the app's form asks for it. The form says "API key": for this printer, say it is the printer's access code. OctoEverywhere's help page for the Centauri Carbon 2 says the code is shown on the printer's touchscreen, in its settings under LAN Only, with LAN Only turned on, and that a printer whose access code is turned off takes the default, 123456 (read 2026-11-16). So a refused test with no key most likely means this printer has a code of its own: a guess from that page, not tried here. Menus change between firmware versions, so if the person does not see LAN Only, search for where their firmware shows the code, and ask them what they see before you name a menu.
- **Any other Elegoo printer, such as a Neptune 4.** The app runs OctoPrint's test. That the Neptune 4 runs Klipper with Moonraker is general knowledge, not tried here: when the Elegoo Link test fails on one, Moonraker at port 7125 is the likeliest next try.

## The address

Ask for the address they open that page at, including any port.

- **Moonraker:** the app needs Moonraker's own address, port 7125 unless it was changed, as in `http://192.168.1.50:7125`. The address of the Mainsail page answered too where that page passed the app's requests on to Moonraker, as a usual Mainsail setup does. A Mainsail page that did not pass them on answered with a web page instead (both seen 2026-11-02 in Docker). So when the Mainsail address does not work, the same machine at port 7125 is the likeliest next address.
- **OctoPrint:** the address they open OctoPrint at.
- The address can be an IP address or a name, but a name this computer cannot look up got no answer at all (seen 2026-11-02 with a `.local` name no device answered to).
- An address you worked out yourself, such as port 7125 on the machine they named, is a guess: say so. When they say to try it, call printer_host_connect with it at once, without asking again.

## The key

printer_host_connect tests the address during the call, for up to 30 seconds, with the key the app already holds for that address or with none. A first try without a key is fine: the answer says whether one is needed. When the host asks for a key, the call stays open and shows the app's key form in the chat. Never ask for the key in chat. The form has three ways out: Connect, which tests again with what they typed; "Help me find the key"; and Cancel. Each ends the call, so its result is the outcome, whichever way it went. When they asked for help finding the key, or closed the form, nothing more was sent, and the result still gives the host's first refusal.

**Moonraker.** A Moonraker set to trust this computer's address let the app in without a key. One that did not answered HTTP 401 Unauthorized, the same answer for no key and for a wrong key (seen 2026-11-02 in Docker), so the result says which key each test sent: none, the one typed in the form, or the one saved for this printer. Most people at home have no key and do not know what one is, so after a 401 do not ask them to type one. What helps them:

- **The likeliest fix on a home network needs no key.** Moonraker lets in only the addresses in `trusted_clients`, under `[authorization]` in `moonraker.conf`, its settings file on the printer's computer. Mainsail's own FAQ for its "connection unauthorized" error says to add the network there, written like `192.168.1.0/24` for the addresses 192.168.1.1 to 192.168.1.254, and then restart Moonraker. That this is their cause is a guess. Where they can edit that file depends on their setup, so search for their version before you say.
- **A key, if they want one.** Moonraker's installation documentation gives the key page as `http://{moonraker-host}/access/api_key`, with no port. The page is Moonraker's own, so it is at Moonraker's address and port, the one that answered 401, as in `http://192.168.1.50:7125/access/api_key`. A page not reached at another port says nothing about the key. The same documentation says to open the page from a trusted client, so a computer Moonraker does not trust may be refused there too. Over SSH on the printer's computer, it gives the script `~/moonraker/scripts/fetch-apikey.sh`.
- Mainsail's FAQ for this error points to `trusted_clients`, not to a key, and no Mainsail or Fluidd page that shows the key was found in their documentation (searched 2026-11-04). Do not send the person looking for one.

**OctoPrint.** It needs a key. Without one, the OctoPrint tried (1.9.3, in Docker, 2026-11-02) answered only to refuse, HTTP 403 "You don't have the permission to access the requested resource". A wrong key got HTTP 403 "Invalid API key", so the two can be told apart. OctoPrint's API documentation says a user's own key is shown in their user settings, and in the user list of its Access Control settings, and the global key in its API settings. Versions differ, so search for where theirs shows it before you say, and ask what they see.

## When it is verified

The result is `verified`, and the app has saved the address as this printer's connection.

- **Moonraker:** the app asked Moonraker for its server information. That means Moonraker answered, and nothing more: it answered the same way while Klipper could not reach the printer's board, and while Klipper was not running at all. What says whether the printer can print is Klipper's state, which the result gives after "Moonraker reports Klipper's state as". Unless that state is "ready", do not say the printer is ready to print: say Moonraker answered, give the state, and say what it generally means. Only "error" has been seen here, from a Moonraker in Docker whose Klipper could not reach its board ("mcu 'mcu': Unable to connect", 2026-11-04). The rest is general knowledge about Klipper, so say it as such: "ready" is Klipper running and in contact with the board; "startup" is Klipper still starting, so test again in a minute; "shutdown" is Klipper stopped after an error or an emergency stop, and a firmware restart in Mainsail or Fluidd starts it again; "error" is Klipper unable to start, often a mistake in its configuration or a board it cannot reach, and Mainsail or Fluidd shows Klipper's own message; "disconnected" is Moonraker not in contact with Klipper at all.
- **OctoPrint:** the app asked OctoPrint for its version. That means OctoPrint answered and took the key, and nothing more: it answered the same way with no printer attached to it.
- **Any other type:** the host answered the app's test the way that test expects, and nothing more. For a Centauri Carbon, that is only its web page naming ELEGOO.

## What the tools report

- `not_configured` means no connection has been saved yet. `unknown` means one is saved and has not been tested in this chat.
- `verified` means the host accepted the test and the app saved the address.
- `failed` comes with what the app's test was told, in the host's own words where it gave any.

## When a connection fails

Say what the app saw in the person's terms, then work out why. What the test was told says which step to suspect. Each of these was seen on 2026-11-02 through the app's own test, against Moonraker, Mainsail and OctoPrint in Docker:

- **HTTP 401 Unauthorized.** Moonraker answered and did not let the app in. The address is right; see the key above.
- **HTTP 403 "You don't have the permission…" or "Invalid API key".** OctoPrint answered and got no key, or refused the one it got. The address is right.
- **HTTP 404.** Something answered at that address, but not as the chosen program answers. This came when OctoPrint was chosen for a Moonraker, and when Moonraker was chosen for an OctoPrint, so the other one at the same address is the next try.
- **"Could not parse Moonraker server response".** A web server answered with a page. This came from a Mainsail page that did not pass requests on. Moonraker's port, 7125, on the same machine is worth trying.
- **"Connection refused".** The machine at that address answered at once, but nothing was listening on that port. The port may be wrong, or the program may not be running.
- **"Connection timed out", after about 10 seconds.** Nothing answered. This came from an address with no device on it, and also from `https://` in front of a server that speaks plain `http://`, so despite what the message says about the network, an `https://` address is worth trying with `http://` first.
- **No answer after 30 seconds.** The test was still waiting. This came from a name ending in `.local` that no device answered to. The IP address, which their router or Mainsail may show, avoids looking up the name.

What is worth trying beyond this has not been tested here, so search for what people with the same setup report before you suggest it. Without a search, general knowledge gives: opening the same address in a browser on this computer, checking the printer's computer and this one are on the same network, or restarting the program. When they want to try again, call printer_host_connect again with the address to use.

## When they are stuck

The JusPrin developers can only fix what they hear about, and they have not tested most setups. A person who has tried and wants them to know can report it with `issue_report_open`, which opens a GitHub issue page in their browser with your summary filled in. It files nothing: they read the page, change it if they like, and submit it with their own GitHub account.

# Writing a connection skill

A connection skill is the text the app adds to a printer chat so the model can guide a person through connecting a printer: `AgentUI/src/skills/connect-bambu/SKILL.md` for Bambu Lab printers, and `connect-print-host/SKILL.md` for every printer that connects through a print host (Moonraker, OctoPrint and the other types `printer_host_connect` takes). Read this before writing a new one or changing one. The general rules for skills, and for when a skill becomes a tool, are in [Tool extension guide, Skills versus tools](mcp-tool-extension-guide.md#skills-versus-tools); this document adds only what connecting a printer needs.

Sentences that describe code or tests describe `jusprin-dev`. Rules marked **Proposed** are not agreed yet; the others carry Kenneth's words or the incident they came from.

## What the skill is for

Kenneth's test, 2026-11-02: the skill is good if the agent guides a person who is stuck and makes educated guesses it labels as guesses, until the printer is connected or the person chooses to leave it. It is not judged by whether a printer connected, by how many states it names, or by whether every sentence in it is true. A skill that is never wrong and never helps a stuck person fails the test.

Three times in three days a skill was written to the wrong half of that test. The first Bambu skill was a table from state to next step, and when a P1S connection failed it told the person to re-check an access code that was right. The second Bambu skill said "add no cause of your own", and the model repeated a false reason instead of guessing. The host skills said "you have not seen where Mainsail or Fluidd show the key", and on 2026-11-04 the model told a person who had no key to look in "Mainsail's settings page", which does not show it. Each time the writer kept "say nothing false" and dropped "help the stuck person".

## How the skill reaches the model

- The app chooses the skill from the saved printer's vendor: a Bambu Lab printer gets `connect-bambu`, any other gets `connect-print-host` (`PrinterConversation::connection_skill`). The model never picks it.
- It is in force as soon as the chat has a saved printer, before the person asks to connect: with `printer_add`'s result, or on the first request of a chat about a saved printer (Kenneth, 2026-11-04). A chat that never connects still carries it, so each skill opens by saying the person may not want to connect, and offers it once after a printer is added.
- It stays in the chat once sent (`AgentSkillUse::stays`).
- `issue_report_open` comes with either skill and is offered from the same request on (Kenneth, 2026-11-06). It opens a GitHub issue page in the person's browser with the model's summary filled in; the person reads it and submits it with their own account. A chat without a connection skill is never offered it.
- The skill opens with "The rules above still apply", so wherever the standing prompt (`AgentUI/src/printerInstructions.ts`) gives an exact sentence or an exact step, the prompt wins over the skill. On 2026-11-04 the prompt's finishing example "It is connected, so you can send prints straight to it" beat the skill's "Moonraker answered, and nothing more", with Klipper shut down. The prompt now keeps only the rules that hold for every printer: the tools act on this printer, connecting is optional, never ask for a credential in chat, and how to finish.

## Before writing: three audits

### 1. The person's stuck moments, not the app's states

Start from the moments a person with this connection type gets stuck, and write to those. The failure table (which result means which step) comes second. The three moments every connection type has:

- **Giving the address, or finding the printer.** What they open in a browser, which port, what if the name does not resolve; for Bambu, why the printer is not heard. The skill is in force before this moment, so it can guide it.
- **Being asked for a credential they do not have.** A Klipper owner who has never heard of an API key; a Bambu owner who cannot find the access code. The skill says, in order of cost to check, what is likeliest and what they can look at, each labelled as observed, documented or a guess. The 401-without-a-key case was the one place both 2026-11-04 Moonraker runs got stuck, when the skill had only "search for where their version shows it".
- **Being told it is connected.** What the app's test proved and did not prove, so the closing sentence does not promise what the app has not checked.

For each moment, write what a competent friend would say to someone standing at that screen. That sentence is the skill's job; the failure table supports it.

### 2. Information against knowledge, per state

Kenneth, 2026-11-02: for each failure, is the cause a lack or wrong *information* (a fact about this situation that only the app can know at that moment) or a lack or wrong *knowledge* (how things work)? Information belongs in the app's note or tool result; knowledge about connecting belongs in the skill; how to work in general belongs in the prompt.

Before writing a line of the skill, list the app's notes and tool results for this connection type and, for each, what the app already holds at that moment that the model would need. Where the result lacks it, the fix is to the result, and the skill is written against the result that will exist. Two gaps found this way on 2026-11-04 are fixed: the Moonraker result now says which key each test sent (none, the one typed in the form, or the saved one), and the verified result gives Klipper's state, which the app read and had only logged.

"Already holds" is the limit. A result forwards what the code has; it does not gain a new probe to tell causes apart ([How to fix a result that hides the failure](mcp-tool-extension-guide.md#how-to-fix-a-result-that-hides-the-failure), rule 2). After 2026-11-02 the Bambu failure note gained a look at the printer's port 8883 before and after each attempt, and the skill gained four cases built on what the port did. The failures it was built to explain came from a development build with Enable SSL(MQTT) off (see [Three kinds of statement](#three-kinds-of-statement-each-labelled)), and both were removed on 2026-11-16.

### 3. The standing prompt and the tool descriptions

List every sentence in `printerInstructions.ts` and in the connection tools' descriptions (`Agent/ToolRegistry.cpp`) that gives an exact wording, an exact step or a procedure for connecting. Each one either goes, becomes conditional, or is accepted knowing the skill cannot override it. On 2026-11-04 four such sentences caused failures the skill's facts should have prevented, and all four have since been removed: the exact offer after `printer_add` (asked a person who had already asked to connect), "say briefly to use that form" after a key was requested (told a person with no key to type one), the finishing example above, and the connect tool's "until they give one, ask for it instead of calling this" (made the model ask permission to try a port the person had just said to try).

This matches [Tool extension guide, A tool description versus a skill](mcp-tool-extension-guide.md#skills-versus-tools): a description that has grown into a step belongs in the skill. The skill work had added new text without sweeping the old. **Proposed:** the sweep is a required step of every connection skill change.

## Writing the skill

### Explain the mechanism as a chain

Number the steps the connection goes through, each depending on the one before, and say so: a step that worked says nothing about the ones after it. This is what let the model reason about failures the skill did not list on 2026-11-03 (an OctoPrint the person called Klipper; `https://` against a plain-http host). Keep the chain from the person's side as well as the app's: for Moonraker, the app reaches Moonraker at its port, and so does the person's browser, so Moonraker's own pages are at that same address and port. A skill that explained only the app's side sent the person to a port-80 URL for the key (2026-11-04).

### Three kinds of statement, each labelled

- **Observed on a real host or printer.** What the app's own test reported, and when. The guard tests in `tests/agent/test_printer_conversation.cpp` require every state the skill names in backquotes to have a dated run behind it. Write these as facts.
- **Documented.** What a maintainer's docs or FAQ say, named ("Mainsail's FAQ for this error says…"). Write these with their source. The evidence rule does not forbid them; leaving them out is what made the host skills silent about the one thing a stuck Klipper owner needs (a 401 from a printer on the same home network is usually fixed in Moonraker's `trusted_clients`, with no key at all).
- **A guess.** General knowledge nobody has checked on this setup. Write it as a guess and give the cheapest check.

An observation counts only from an app set up the way people get it. Every "real P1S" result before 2026-11-04 came from a development build with Enable SSL(MQTT) off in the app's settings, which logs in to the printer without TLS: code -1 with the right access code, and a failure about 24 seconds after the attempt began. A release build takes TLS from the printer, and with the setting on the same P1S connected in about a second. The skill, its guard and the prompt cases stated those artifacts as facts for two weeks. **Proposed:** before a run on a real printer is recorded as observed, the record says which build ran it and, for a development build, the settings that differ from a release build.

What not to write, each from an incident:

- One next step per state. The state-to-step table sent a person with the right code to re-check it (P1S, 2026-11-02).
- "Add no cause of your own" or anything that forbids reasoning. The model repeated a false reason (P1S, 2026-11-02). The guard bans the phrase.
- A menu path as fact (`Settings > WLAN`). The guard bans arrows and "Settings >".

content.text:
Only part of it. A skill is text the model reads, so it can change what the AI says and which tools it calls. It can't give the app a capability the tools don't have, and two of the three missing pieces are capabilities.

There is no separate Flashforge skill today. The app sends a Bambu Lab printer the `connect-bambu` skill and every other printer `connect-print-host`, choosing between them by the printer's vendor (`PrinterConversation::connection_skill`, [PrinterConversation.cpp:461](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/PrinterSetup/PrinterConversation.cpp:461)). So a Creator 5 Pro owner gets the general print-host skill.

**What a skill can't do**

Say the model has a perfect Flashforge skill and knows it needs the serial number and the access code. It still can't hand them over:

- `printer_host_connect` takes only `hostType` and `address`. It has no field for a serial number, and the AI is blocked from writing `flashforge_serial_number` as a setting.
- The access-code form opens only when the printer answers HTTP 401 or 403. Without a serial number, the app's Flashforge test goes to port 8899, and a Creator 5 Pro refuses that connection, so the form never opens.
- Nothing in the chat runs Flashforge's network search. That search is the one that finds the serial number for the person.

The guide for connection skills draws the same line ([connection-skill-guide.md](agent-docs/jusprin/connection-skill-guide.md), the "information against knowledge" audit). Knowledge about how a connection works belongs in the skill. A fact only the app can get, such as the serial number from the network search, belongs in a tool result. Searching the network and opening the form are app code.

**What a skill can do (proposal)**

1. **Today, with no tool change:** add Flashforge to the skill's list of connection types the chat can't finish. That list already sends Repetier, UltiMaker and PrusaLink with a password to the app's own window: View › Switch to classic view…, then the Wi-Fi icon beside "Printer". From OrcaSlicer's code ([PhysicalPrinterDialog.cpp:702](src/slic3r/GUI/PhysicalPrinterDialog.cpp:702)), choosing Flashforge in that window shows a serial number field and an access code field. It also has a Discover button that fills in the serial number. The reporter could finish there now. I haven't run that window with a real Flashforge printer.
2. **Once the tools can do it:** a Flashforge section in the skill. It would say that the Creator 5 and Adventurer 5 series need a serial number and an access code, where the person finds the code on the printer's screen, and that OctoPrint is the wrong type for these printers. That would have stopped the reporter's chat from trying OctoPrint on port 80. Under the skill's evidence rule, the observed parts need a run against a real printer first, which we don't have. Until then they'd be written as what the docs say or as labelled guesses.

The full fix is still the tool change from my first answer: the network search fills in the serial number, and the access-code form opens up front for Flashforge. The skill would explain that step to the person. It can't stand in for it.

The earlier session did open the tool to every connection type. The tool accepts Flashforge, and I was wrong to make it sound like it refuses it. What that session missed is that Flashforge needs a third setting, the printer's serial number, that the chat never fills in. Here is how that happened.

**The session and what it did**

The session is [Issue 40: connect Elegoo Centauri Carbon from the chat](#local_d4756db3-d543-4cd9-82bf-8127f6b55132), and its work is commit f88b40865c from 2026-11-16. Before that commit, the chat refused every type except Moonraker and OctoPrint. You told it "To every type." It added Flashforge and the others to the tool's list and let each run OrcaSlicer's own connection test.

So when the Creator 5 Pro owner chose Flashforge, the app did run OrcaSlicer's Flashforge test. The test failed because the chat saved only three settings: the type, the address and one key (`configure_named_printer_host`). Without a serial number, OrcaSlicer's test skips the printer's HTTP interface and tries the old port 8899, which this printer refuses.

**Why those three types are in the skill's list**

You described that list as the types the chat can finish. It's the reverse: it's the types the chat can't finish. The rationale is in the commit message and the skill text. The chat sends an address and one key, so any type whose OrcaSlicer test reads more than that can't be completed in the chat:

- Repetier also reads which printer is chosen on the host.
- UltiMaker reads a user name and password.
- PrusaLink set up with a password reads a user name and password.

The skill sends those people to the classic printer window instead. Flashforge belongs on the same list for the same reason, and the session missed it.

**Why it missed Flashforge**

The session built the list from one code search across OrcaSlicer's connection code. The search looked for settings whose names start with `print_host` or `printhost`, read the usual way. Flashforge reads its serial number as `flashforge_serial_number`, through a helper of its own (`safe_config_string`, [Flashforge.cpp:230](src/slic3r/Utils/Flashforge.cpp:230)). The search matched neither the name nor the helper, so Flashforge didn't appear in its results at all.

The session had also printed `Flashforge::test` twice a few minutes earlier, including the line that only uses the HTTP interface when a serial number is set. It never connected that to the list. In its notes it only checked whether each test opens a window and whether the type is an online service.

I reran the check with a wider search. Flashforge is the only connection type whose test reads a setting the chat never fills in and that the skill doesn't mention. CrealityPrint reads a port setting too, but its test doesn't use it.

**What this means for the fix (proposal)**

Two steps are still needed:

- Add Flashforge to the skill's list of types the chat can't finish, now.
- Make the chat able to finish a Flashforge connection: the network search fills in the serial number, and the access-code form opens up front. Because this adds a step to printer setup, it starts with design boards.

**Timings on this Mac, Release config, load 30 to 40:** fresh worktree build of `jusprin_web jusprin_catalogs agent_bridge_tests workspace_contract_tests setting_display_tests shell_integration_harness` was 905 steps in about 14 min; the shell harness default regression (549 checks) about 2 min; the workspace adapter harness (972 checks) under 1 min. See [[jusprin-worktree-build]], [[live-test-built-app-on-mac]].

**Seeding a preset (2026-10-12).** `--manual-mcp` does not wipe its directory at start, so a user preset written to `<fixture>/user/default/machine/<name>.json` before launch (keys `from: User`, `inherits`, `name`, `printer_settings_id`, `version`, plus the values under test) is loaded and can be named as a settings `target.preset`. A Python driver that starts the harness with `subprocess.Popen` and terminates it in `finally` avoids Trap 1.


**Why a plate will not slice (2026-10-15).** MCP `slice_report` on a plate Orca refuses says only `valid: false`, with no reason even with `sections: ["findings"]`, and `slice_start` still answers `started: true`. Orca's own refusal text is in `<fixture>/log/debug_*.log`: grep `validate err=`. Used to reproduce the PETG HF on Smooth Cool Plate case (branch `claude/bed-type-mismatch`, worktree distracted-lehmann-9c1b12). See [[printer-setup-bed-type-check]].

**Slice waits, 2026-10-15 (jusprin-newui 336facf825).** Trap 2 re-measured: `slice_start {plateId, wait: true}` on the sliced, unchanged plate 1 got no reply in 120 s (a hang, follow-up task filed). Right after `printer_setup` fixes a plate Orca had refused, `slice_start` fails "That plate cannot be sliced as it stands" for about 3 s: the adapter checks `PartPlate::can_slice()`, whose invalid flag Orca refreshes only on its next deferred validation. A refused slice hanging the wait was fixed on branch `claude/slice-wait-refused` (worktree brave-panini-347b62): `WorkspaceSlicing::refused` carries Orca's ValidateError text. name: live-test-built-app-on-mac
description: "How to launch, see, and drive the locally built JusPrin app on the Mac: the shared bundle id binds tools to the wrong instance, and \"on another Space\" usually means the window is on the second monitor, not that the user is in full screen."
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: fa2d66ed-e217-440b-aae0-da4164953edc
  modified: 2026-11-01T19:29:08.107Z
---

Every build of the fork (and /Applications/OrcaSlicer.app) shares bundle id `com.softfever3d.orca-slicer`. The desktop-control tools resolve an app by bundle id and bind to whichever instance comes first, so `app_list_windows` returns `[]` and filtered screenshots hide the window you actually launched.

**Working recipe (2026-09-05):** `ditto` the built .app into the scratchpad, `plutil -replace CFBundleIdentifier -string com.jusprin.worktree-test`, `codesign --force --deep -s -`, then `open -n <copy>.app --args <model>` and `request_access` for the new id. `app_screenshot`/`app_click` then work and include popup menus. A display-scope `left_click` on the header did NOT open the fork's PopupWindow menus, but a background `app_click` did; take the pixel-level `zoom` with the display tools afterwards (call `app_release` first). Display-scope `Escape` does not close those popups; a click elsewhere does.

The MCP discovery file `~/Library/Application Support/JusPrin2/jusprin/mcp.json` points at the newest instance's `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/mcp`; `tests/mcp/probe.py`'s `call()` can drive real tools (e.g. `workspace_inspect`, then `report_slice_review` with sessionId/plateId/sliceResultId) to put the header into the Check-print state without lldb. lldb `expr` cannot call inline accessors like `status_row()`.

**Why:** On 2026-09-01 a verification pass screenshotted the stock app instead of the build; on 2026-09-05 the tools bound to another session's main-repo build.

**How to apply:** Confirm the pid with `pgrep -fl OrcaSlicer.app/Contents/MacOS`; never kill an instance you did not launch. `osascript` System Events by unix id still works to set `frontmost`. See [[jusprin-shell-phase-1-design]] and [[orca-inherited-teardown-crash]].

**"On another Space" usually means "on the other monitor."** Cost about ten turns on
2026-09-09 and produced a wrong report to Kenneth. `app_list_windows` returns
`is_off_space: true` and clicks are refused with "this window is on another Space";
`app_bring_to_current_space` then fails with "the user's current Space is a full-screen
app." Both messages are about Spaces, so the natural read is that the user is sitting in
a full-screen app — but with *Displays have separate Spaces* on, a window merely sitting
on the second monitor produces exactly the same symptoms. Kenneth was not in full screen;
the harness had opened on the Acer.

Tell them apart before saying anything to the user: take a **display-scope** screenshot
(`app_release`, then `computer_batch` screenshot). Its header names the monitor it
captured and lists the others — if the window shows up there, it is a monitor problem,
not a Space problem, and the display-scope tools can drive it immediately. Never conclude
"the user is in a full-screen app" from the background tools' error text alone.

The same flag also flaps: a window can read `is_off_space: false` and click fine, then
read `true` a minute later. Clicks delivered while it is true report `ok ... unverified`
and silently do nothing. **A click that reports "unverified" and changes nothing is not
evidence of an application bug** — on 2026-09-09 that nearly became a filed defect about
being unable to retry after a failed MCP connect. Re-verify on a reachable window before
concluding anything about the app.

**Prefer the shell harness over a re-signed app copy for Agent-panel work.**
`tests/shell/.../JusPrinShellHarness.app` already carries its own bundle id
(`io.jusprin.shell-harness`), so none of the bundle-id collision above applies, and
`--manual-unconfigured` lands directly on the dock's not-set-up state — one click from
the Agent setup chooser. Build target is `shell_integration_harness`, not `shell_harness`.

**Isolate `$HOME` when testing MCP client setup.** `Mcp::default_catalog_paths()` reads
`$HOME`, so the flow will happily rewrite the real `~/.cursor/mcp.json`. Launch with
`HOME=<scratch>` holding a `.cursor/mcp.json` fixture; detection, the diff, and the write
all follow it. Force a write failure with `chmod 444` on the file **and** `555` on its
directory — the directory alone is not enough.

**Re-signed copies trigger system prompts.** Each rebuild + ad-hoc re-sign changes the cdhash, so macOS re-asks for Downloads access (recent-project thumbnail load blocks in `fopen`) and Keychain access (agent runtime reads the API key). Both are prompts only the user can answer. Avoid them by running the binary directly (`nohup <copy>.app/Contents/MacOS/OrcaSlicer --datadir <scratch copy of JusPrin2 with recent_projects cleared> <model>`) with `OPENAI_API_KEY=<placeholder>` in the environment, which short-circuits the Keychain lookup in `AgentConfiguration.cpp`. Use `sample <pid>` on the main thread to see which prompt is blocking.

**Stale as of 2026-09-18 (branch claude/printer-conversation-panel-af11cb):** `load_agent_runtime` reads the key only from app config (`jusprin_agent` / `openai_api_key`); no env var or Keychain lookup exists there. In the shell harness, `OPENAI_API_KEY` only feeds the docked pane via `install_harness_agent`; the printer panel builds its own runtime from app config, so `--printer-live` writes the key into the run's throwaway conf. Pass it as `std::string`: `AppConfig::set(section, key, const char*)` silently picks the `bool` overload and stores `true` (seen as a 401 "key rejected"). The harness temp data dir then holds the real key: delete `/var/folders/*/*/T/jusprin-shell-*` dirs from those runs afterwards.

**Hands-on printer panel with a live model (2026-09-23, jusprin-newui, uncommitted at the time):** `--manual-live-agent` now also writes `OPENAI_API_KEY` into the run's app config, so Home → "+ Add printer" gets a live printer chat. Feed the key from `~/Library/Application Support/JusPrin2/JusPrin2.conf` (`jusprin_agent.openai_api_key`) via env without echoing it. Drive it with display-scope `computer_batch` clicks/typing (background `app_click` does nothing on the web view). The scripted `--printer-live` run hangs when the model doesn't pick the printer its next "tap" step expects; kill it. Afterwards `rm -rf` the run's `/var/folders/*/*/T/jusprin-shell-*` dir — killed runs leave it behind with the key.

**Give each automated harness run a fresh scratch `$HOME`.** On 2026-09-09 a second run
against a reused scratch `$HOME` (and with a `jusprin-mcp` helper left over from the
first) never got past the Agent page handshake: it printed `HARNESS WAIT
agent_bridge_handshake preview=0 plate=0 slice_valid=1` about twice a second forever and
had to be killed at ten minutes. Runs before and after it, each with a freshly created
`$HOME` and a `pkill -f jusprin-mcp` first, finished with zero `HARNESS WAIT` lines at
all. **The cause was not isolated** — reuse and the stale helper were not separated, so
treat this as a recipe, not an explanation. `rm -rf` and recreate the scratch `$HOME`,
`pkill -f jusprin-mcp`, then run; if the handshake wait appears anyway, kill it early
rather than assuming the change under test broke the bridge.

**2026-09-19 addendum:** background `app_click` on the Home/Agent WKWebViews reports
"ok … unverified" and nothing happens; only display-scope `computer_batch` clicks
reach the page. The re-signed copy opened on the *Built-in Retina Display* while the
display tools default to the Acer, so `switch_display` first. `Return` in the composer
sends in the real app; in the built-in-browser fixture it does not (click the send
button). Another Claude session holding the computer-use lock blocks `request_access`
until Kenneth stops that session. Page-only states are cheaper via [[fake-host-page-fixture]].

**2026-10-28: background clicks no longer open header popups.** In `--manual`, background `app_click` on the printer chip (body or chevron) left the chip pressed but no menu appeared, and `--printer-menu-capture`'s screen blit came back solid black with the screen unlocked (likely a rebuilt binary losing screen-recording permission). For header menu rows, use `HeaderButton::snapshot(2.0)` in the harness instead (see `ring_dashes` in `capture_chip_appearance`).

**Modal dialogs ignore synthetic input (2026-10-28).** OrcaSlicer's own modal dialogs (Send print job, Previously opened file) took no click or key from computer-use in either mode: background app_click is refused ("belongs to a different process") and display clicks/keys do nothing, though log/AX showed the dialog topmost and the app idle. Kenneth's real click on Send worked at once. Web-view screens (Home cards) and menu shortcuts (Cmd+R slice, Cmd+Shift+G send dialog) do work. So when a step needs a modal's button, ask Kenneth to press it and watch the log; don't spend turns on monitors or overlays. Also: launch the copy with `open -n <copy>.app --args --datadir …`, never the binary from the shell (that instance took no input at all), and trim the datadir's `recent_projects` to non-Downloads paths or startup stalls on a macOS Downloads-access prompt.

**Header popups and Open dialogs (2026-11-01).** A background `app_click` on a chip half opens its popup only while the app is frontmost: set frontmost with System Events by unix id, click, find the popup's id with a `CGWindowListCopyWindowInfo` lister (layer 101), then `app_screenshot` that raw id. File > Open's panel belongs to another process, and computer-use refuses input to it and says not to work around that; open the file with the MCP `project_open` tool instead (`load_project(path, "<loadall>")`, against File > Open's `"-"`) and say so. lldb on the RelWithDebInfo build reads and forces flags without touching code: `(Slic3r::GUI::GUI_App*)wxApp::ms_appInstance`, then `preset_bundle->printers.m_edited_preset`; read the Print's flags with a breakpoint on `Print::validate`, because `plater_->p->fff_print` still holds default settings.

name: scratch-app-driving-traps
description: "Traps met driving a scratch copy of the built app without screen control: in-place binary copy gets SIGKILL, Home drops bridge messages while hidden, header popups need a posted NSEvent, lldb std::string args and @import failures, the model picker needs page JS, a debugger attach once hung a slice."
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: reference
  originSessionId: dea8379c-b02c-43a2-a254-4c2259672439
  modified: 2026-11-12T18:04:04.144Z
---

Met while verifying print-host printer window fixes on the scratch `.app` (see [[live-test-built-app-on-mac]], [[open-file-in-app-without-screen-control]]).

- **Copy a new build into a `.app` with `rm` then `cp`.** `cp` over the existing signed binary keeps the inode; the kernel kills the launch at once (exit 137, nothing logged).
- **A launch from a plain Bash call dies when the call ends.** Start the app with `run_in_background: true` and `exec`.
- **Home ignores bridge messages while the main window shows a project.** A queued `launch_monitor` through `JUSPRIN_HOME_DEV_URL` is sent by the page and silently dropped; switch to Home first (`m_tabpanel->SetSelection(0)` via lldb).
- **Background `app_click` does not reach the header's popup menus** (they are not listed as windows). Post the click into the app's queue with lldb: `expr -l objc -- @import AppKit`, then `NSEvent mouseEventWithType:NSEventTypeLeftMouseDown/Up location:NSMakePoint(x, y-from-popup-bottom) ... windowNumber:[popup windowNumber]` and `[NSApp postEvent:atStart:NO]`. Render the popup with `cacheDisplayInRect:` on its contentView ([[capture-mac-popups-for-platform-diff]]).
- **lldb cannot build `std::string` args.** This libc++ uses the alternate short-string layout: a 24-byte char array with the text at offset 0 and its length in byte 23 (≤ 22 chars), passed as `*(std::string*)buf`.
- **wx `wxStaticText::Wrap()` (Orca's wx) skips a width it already wrapped at and keeps the first text it wrapped**, so SetLabel + Wrap on a reused label comes back unwrapped. Use a fresh label.
- **With the screen locked, an instrumented dev page stops polling** (WebKit throttles the hidden page's timers; `document.visibilityState` is "hidden"). Run JS in it through lldb instead: walk `[NSApp windows]` → subviews to the `WKWebView` (match its title or `URL`), then `[webview evaluateJavaScript:@"…" completionHandler:nil]`; the page can `fetch()` results to the dev server. A menu item without a shortcut: `[[item target] performSelector:[item action] withObject:item afterDelay:0.5]` from lldb, so the modal it opens runs after detach.
- **`@import AppKit` can fail silently in lldb `expr`** ("no known method '-windows'"). Then cast everything to `id` and get classes with `((Class(*)(const char*))objc_getClass)("NSApplication")`; a working runner that runs a JS file in the chat panel (title "JusPrin Agent") was `runjs.sh` in the 2026-11-12 scratchpad.
- **The composer's model picker is a drop-down the background `app_click` refuses.** Click it from page JS via the runner above. OpenRouter's list labels models "Anthropic: Claude …", so a regex on "Claude Fable" picks OpenRouter's copy; the Anthropic-key one starts with "Claude".
- **A slice right after lldb attaches hung once (2026-11-12).** The worker sat in upstream `name_tbb_thread_pool_threads_set_locale()`, a barrier every TBB thread must reach, and the main thread waited in `BackgroundSlicingProcess::start()` forever. After a relaunch with no debugger the same slice ran at once. Suspected trigger: pausing the app while its thread pool was starting. Don't report such a hang as an app bug without a run that had no debugger attached.
- **A locked screen slows the whole app 2-4×** (2026-11-05: the same first-launch OrcaSlicer import took 46 s unlocked at 15:48, 226 s locked at 19:22, same build and folder). Compare timings only between back-to-back runs under the same conditions, old and new builds side by side.

name: jusprin-worktree-build
description: How to configure a JusPrin worktree build reusing existing deps; BUILD_TESTS=ON needed for tests
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: reference
  originSessionId: 01c34c35-1546-40fb-a600-c49b2e1ffa06
  modified: 2026-09-18T23:36:14.653Z
---

A JusPrin git worktree builds against the already-built deps by configuring:

```
cmake -B build/arm64 -G "Ninja Multi-Config" -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DCMAKE_OSX_ARCHITECTURES=arm64 -DCMAKE_OSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET=15.0 \
  -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/deps/build/arm64/OrcaSlicer_dep/usr/local \
  -DSLIC3R_GUI=ON -DSLIC3R_STATIC=ON -DSLIC3R_PCH=ON -DBUILD_TESTS=ON \
  -DCMAKE_AR=/opt/homebrew/opt/llvm/bin/llvm-ar -DCMAKE_RANLIB=/opt/homebrew/opt/llvm/bin/llvm-ranlib
```

ONE PREFIX PATH (2026-11-15): since the 2.5.0 merge, CMakeLists.txt finds its bundled Python under CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH + /libpython; a two-entry list fails configure with "Bundled Python executable not found under <a;b>/libpython/bin". Pass only the JusPrin deps path (as other worktrees' caches do).

CMAKE BINARY (2026-09-29): configure with `/Applications/CMake.app/Contents/bin/cmake` (put it first on PATH). Homebrew's cmake 4.1 at /opt/homebrew/bin fails with "Could NOT find Eigen3 (missing: EIGEN3_VERSION_OK) (Required is at least version 5.0.1)", and a failed configure poisons the cache: `rm -rf build` before retrying.

The two `CMAKE_AR`/`CMAKE_RANLIB` flags are required on a FRESH build dir:
without them Apple's ar is used and liblibslic3r_gui.a (>4 GiB in
RelWithDebInfo) fails to archive. They only work at first configure, not on
reconfigure. Full story: agent-docs/macos-build-troubleshooting.md. See
[[liblibslic3r-gui-4gib-ar-limit]].

FRESH WORKTREE TRAP (2026-09-18): building only `shell_integration_harness`
does not build the web pages. Also build `--target jusprin_web jusprin_catalogs`
(needs node on PATH: /Users/kenneth/.nvm/versions/node/v24.13.0/bin). Without
them resources/jusprin/{home,agent}/index.html are missing, no web views are
created, and the harness silently tests something else (printer panel starts
shown; web-view crashes vanish).

`BUILD_TESTS=ON` is required or the tests/ tree (workspace, shell targets) is
not generated. Build with `cmake --build build/arm64 --config RelWithDebInfo
--target <targets>`. wxWidgets 3.3 sources for API verification live under
/Users/kenneth/Projects/OrcaSlicer/deps/build/arm64/dep_wxWidgets-prefix/.

CWD TRAP (cost real time once): the harness resets the Bash cwd to the main
repo /Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin between turns, so a *relative*
`cmake --build build/arm64` silently builds the MAIN repo's build dir, not the
worktree's — the worktree binary then runs stale code and a re-fix looks like it
"didn't take". Always pass the worktree build dir as an ABSOLUTE path to
`cmake --build /…/.claude/worktrees/<wt>/build/arm64 …`, and run test binaries by
absolute path. Also: `cmake --build --target <one_exe>` may relink against a
stale lib without recompiling a changed .cpp in that lib — build the app target
(e.g. OrcaSlicer) too so the lib recompiles; verify with
`grep -c '<file>.cpp.o' build.log`. Editing tools (Edit/Write) use absolute
paths so source edits land correctly regardless of cwd.

STALE PROMPT TRAP (2026-09-23): `--target shell_integration_harness` does NOT
rebuild the web pages, so a harness run after an edit to AgentUI (for example
printerInstructions.ts) loads the old bundle. Six --printer-live runs were
wasted this way. After any page edit, build `jusprin_web` explicitly and check

result.output: # JusPrin design guidelines **Status:** Canonical guidance for `jusprin-dev` on how a screen gets designed and checked, and on the words it shows. The visual system (tokens, type, color, components, logo) lives in [Design system](design-system.md); this document does not repeat it. Design agents tend to write on-screen text that only they can read. The agent knows how the screen works, so a line like "The sixth digit signs you in." reads clearly to it and to any reviewer who knows the same. A person opening the app for the first time has to decode it, and often can't. The First-Launch Confusion Review (https://claude.ai/artifact/91wmdS3QU8UkzbPi1zog15, 2026-11-06) found 23 places on the first launch where a newcomer would misread or stall, and most of them were wording. The rules below exist to stop that at the source and to catch what still gets through. ## How a screen gets designed and checked These steps apply to every change to text a person sees, not only to new screens: a new link on an existing board, a reworded line, or a one-sentence fix all get the cold-reader check on the board before building (step 5) and in the running app after (step 8). 1. **Start from the person.** Before drawing, write down in two or three sentences who reaches this screen, what they know at that moment, what they came to do, and what they must decide here. Every line on the screen serves one of those. 2. **Draw the whole screen, not a component alone.** A board for review is the full screen at the app's size, with the header, panes and neighbouring content the person really sees there, on the JusPrin v2 canvas (https://claude.ai/artifact/ENCtdaz7gjynfbcy4JYbWJ). Build it from the Design System artifact's coded components and the app's own markup, never by copying an older board. Repeated compositions are imported by name, as [Design handoff requirements](design-system.md#design-handoff-requirements) rule 9 says. 3. **Fill it with real strings.** Text that summarises data comes from the rule that will produce it in the app, run on real data. If only a model could write a line, say so on the board. 4. **Write every line by the wording rule below.** 5. **Run the cold-reader check on the boards** (below). Rewrite and check again until every line and button reads as intended. 6. **Show the board for review by what a person sees.** Name the screen as the person would ("the welcome screen, after typing an email"), give the canvas page it is on, and attach the picture. Board ids and builder labels mean nothing to a reviewer. 7. **Build it** following [Writing UI code](design-system.md#writing-ui-code). 8. **Check it in the running app.** Take screenshots of the built screen along one real path and run the cold-reader check again. The guards prove the code went through the tokens; only the screenshots show what the person reads. ## The cold-reader check The writer of a screen cannot see that its text is cryptic, so the check is done by a reader who knows nothing about how the screen works. - Start a fresh agent. Give it only the screenshots and one or two sentences a real user would know (for example: "You own a 3D printer and just installed JusPrin, a desktop app that prepares 3D models for printing."). Give it no code, spec, design notes, chat history or list of suspected problems, and rename files so their names don't hint at anything. - Use screenshots from one coherent path, in the order a person meets them. Mixing signed-in and signed-out screens, or states set by hand, makes the reader report contradictions that no user would see. - Ask it, for each screen, to quote every line and every button exactly, say in one plain sentence what the line means or what the button will do, and list where it would hesitate, misread, worry, or not know what to do next, including information the screen leaves out. Tell it to read literally, like a busy newcomer: a line it had to puzzle out counts as a problem even if it worked it out. - Compare its answers with the intent written in step 1. Any line it reads differently from the intent gets rewritten, however small the gap. Its other hesitations are input to weigh, not orders. What the check is known to catch: on 2026-11-06 a fresh agent given only the review's ten screenshots fully caught 14 of the 23 problems and partly caught 4 more. It caught every cryptic phrasing in the list. It missed problems that need knowledge from outside the screen (that Skip installs a 250 mm Klipper printer) and finer editorial calls (a redundant reassurance, one allowance under three names, "Connected" used for an account). It also raised real questions the review had not, such as what happens after the free month. It has not been compared with a real first-time user, so for the screens that matter most, such as first launch, a person remains the final test. ## Wording Every line says what the person does or what happens to them, in a full sentence, in words a newcomer already has. The five patterns below are what the review found most. Each pair is the text the app showed and the review's proposed rewrite; the rewrites are proposals, not yet in the app. 1. **Facts joined by a middle dot.** The dot drops how the facts relate, and the reader guesses. - Before: "Signed in as new@example.com · 500 credits" (reads like a balance the person already had) - After: "You got 500 free credits for signing up.", with the email address on a smaller line under it 2. **Metaphors.** The reader has to work out what the image stands for. - Before: "New or existing account, same door." - After: a "Sign up free" button, with "Already have an account? Sign in" under it - Before: "Pick how the agent should think." (the options are ways to pay for or connect the agent) - After: "Sign up to use the AI agent, or skip it and just slice." 3. **Describing the mechanism instead of the action.** Say what the person does, not how the screen works inside. - Before: "The sixth digit signs you in. Read the email on any device." - After: "Type the code from the email. You can open it on your phone." 4. **Internal labels.** A name the team uses, shown nowhere else on the screen, explains nothing. - Before: "An Expert message is 5 credits." - After: the cost in things the person does, for example "500 credits is about 100 questions to the agent" (check the number against real costs) 5. **Hinting at a consequence instead of stating it.** If a choice changes what the person gets, say what it changes. - Before: "Skip, and JusPrin slices for a generic 0.4 mm printer until you add yours." - After: "If you skip, files are sliced for a stand-in printer with a 250 mm bed, not for yours. Add your printer before you print anything. You can do that later on the home screen." Space on a screen is tight, and short text looks finished. That is how these lines get written. Shorten only after the full sentence passes the cold-reader check, and check again after shortening. --- name: show-design-in-the-screen description: "Kenneth, 2026-10-28: a design board for review must show the change inside the whole screen it lives in (real viewport, the pane, the header), never a component drawn alone; he rejected header-strip-only boards as drawn 'out of thin air in the vacuum'." metadata: node_type: memory type: feedback originSessionId: 4219b55f-d6b6-4807-b23b-1c973a54c315 modified: 2026-10-28T15:41:05.547Z --- On 2026-10-28 I published four boards for the "from the file" printer-chip mark: the header strip alone, the chip's states, the menu popover, the header after a choice.
